title: 1 Timothy
subtitle: Order for God's household, and mercy for the first of sinners
lead: A letter in Paul's name to Timothy, his younger coworker, left in charge at Ephesus to stop teachers who had gone wrong and to set the church's life in order. It covers prayer for all people, men and women at worship, the qualities of overseers and deacons, the care of widows, the pay and discipline of elders, slaves and the rich, and the danger of the love of money. Through it all runs one picture: the church as "the household of God," holding up the truth about Christ.

It is also one of the most argued-over books of the New Testament. Most critical scholars think a follower of Paul wrote it after his death; the traditional view, still held by many, is that Paul wrote it late in his life. And its words on women (2:11-15), on married clergy (3:2) and on ordination (4:14) stand behind real differences between the churches today. This edition lays out each view and lets the reader weigh them.
facts: Traditionally Paul; many scholars think a later follower writing in his name (see below)
Traditional view: the early or middle 60s, between two Roman imprisonments. Critical view: late first or early second century
Ephesus, chief city of the Roman province of Asia; Paul has gone on to Macedonia (1:3)
A letter of instruction from a leader to a delegate, meant to be read to the church
authorship: The letter names Paul (1:1) and was read as his from the second century: Irenaeus quotes 1:4 as the words of "the apostle," and Polycarp's letter has wording very close to 6:7 and 6:10, which Holmes, Berding and Hartog judge to be use of 1 Timothy (from "high probability" to "certain"). Defenders explain the different style by the different audience (a trusted coworker, not a young church), by Paul's age and new problems, or by a secretary. They place the letter after Acts 28: Paul was released, "sent again upon the ministry of preaching," and martyred on a second stay in Rome, as Eusebius (Church History 2.22) relates. Modern defenders of Paul's authorship include Luke Timothy Johnson (Anchor Bible, 2001) and Philip Towner (New International Commentary on the New Testament).

Friedrich Schleiermacher questioned 1 Timothy in 1807; since then most critical scholars have come to hold that all three Pastoral Letters come from a follower of Paul writing in his name, with dates proposed from the late first to the middle of the second century. P. N. Harrison (1921) argued from the vocabulary, much of it absent from Paul's other letters and common in second-century writers. Other arguments: settled church offices; "the faith" as a body of teaching to guard; opponents who resemble later groups (6:20); travels hard to fit into Paul's life as Acts tells it; and a more restrictive view of women than Romans 16 and 1 Corinthians 11:5 suggest. I. Howard Marshall (International Critical Commentary) is among those who conclude that Paul did not write it.

Some think genuine notes of Paul were worked into the letters, especially into 2 Timothy; others, that a close associate wrote with Paul's approval (Ben Witherington: "the voice is the voice of Paul, but the hand is the hand of Luke"). Whether writing in a revered teacher's name was acceptable is itself debated: Marshall calls it "allonymity," authorship by another person with no intent to deceive, and Richard Bauckham has argued that such writing was not normally forgery; Bart Ehrman (2012) argues that ancient critics, pagan, Jewish and Christian, treated false claims of authorship as deceit. The topic page on the Pastoral Letters sets out both sides.

The papyrus P46 (about AD 200), our oldest collection of Paul's letters, has lost its last leaves, so whether it contained the Pastorals cannot be known; its first editor, Kenyon, judged there was not room. Tertullian (Against Marcion 5.21) says Marcion rejected the letters to Timothy and Titus. The Muratorian list includes them.

audience.to: Timothy, Paul's longtime coworker from Lystra (Acts 16:1-3), left in charge of the house churches of Ephesus, and through him the churches themselves, who would hear the letter read aloud. They were a mixed and established community: households with masters and slaves, wealthy patrons and poor widows, elders some of whom were paid, and teachers who had gone wrong, some of them named.
audience.why: To give Timothy written authority to stop teachers who mixed the law with myths and speculation, forbade marriage and foods, and made money from religion; and to set the household of God in order so that it would hold up the truth and give outsiders no reason to slander it. Knowing that the letter was read aloud explains why a note to one man reads like a church order: every group in the church was meant to hear what was asked of it.
views: A real letter for a real crisis at Ephesus in the 60s, giving a young delegate the backing of his absent teacher.
A later letter for later churches
A follower of Paul writes in his name to the churches of Asia some decades later, using Paul and Timothy as the model of how sound teaching and church order are handed on.

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads the letter against Ephesus in the first century: its households, slaves and patrons, its widows, its temple of Artemis, and the teachers the letter opposes.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks who wrote the Pastoral Letters and when, how their church order compares with Paul's undisputed letters, and what the opponents and the text's history reveal.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Follows how the letter is built: the alternation of 'some' and 'you', the trustworthy sayings, the hymn of 3:16, the doxologies, and the household picture that ties it together.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads the letter alongside the law it quotes (the Ten Commandments, Deuteronomy 25:4 and 19:15), Jewish care of widows, synagogue elders and reading, and Jewish praise of the one God.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: How the churches have read and used the letter: election (2:4), the one mediator (2:5), women in ministry (2:11-15), married clergy (3:2), women deacons (3:11), ordination (4:14), and the deposit of faith (6:20).

sections.b:
Read it as a letter meant to be overheard. It is addressed to Timothy, but nearly every instruction is about someone else: men and women at prayer, overseers, deacons, widows and their families, elders, slaves, the rich. The church would hear the letter read and know what was asked of each group, and that Timothy spoke with Paul's authority.

Read it, too, as a letter at war. The instructions are written against teachers who had gone wrong (1:3-7; 4:1-5; 6:3-10, 20-21). Much that sounds like general rules makes most sense as an answer to them: the stress on marriage and childbearing against those who forbade marriage, the stress on food as God's good gift against those who forbade foods, the stress on quiet and order against "empty talk" and arguments.

Some key words appear often here and seldom in Paul's other letters. "Godliness" (eusebeia): reverence for God lived out in an ordered life. "Sound teaching": literally "healthy" teaching, against the "sick" craving for arguments (6:4). "This saying is trustworthy": a formula that marks known sayings (1:15; 3:1; 4:9). "God our Savior." "The appearing" (epiphaneia) of Christ. The Plain renders each of these the same way in all three Pastoral Letters.

Four passages carry most of the weight of later debate. 2:11-15 on women teaching and holding authority; 3:2 and 3:12 on "the husband of one wife"; 3:11 on "women likewise" among the deacons; and 6:1-2 on slaves. Each has a full note, and the chapter pages set out the readings and the churches' positions side by side. On each, faithful Christians disagree, and this edition does not rank them.

1 Timothy stands with 2 Timothy and Titus as the "Pastoral Letters," a name that became common in the 1700s. In Bibles they come after 1 and 2 Thessalonians because Paul's letters to churches come first and his letters to individuals after them, each group roughly from longest to shortest. The churches have received 1 Timothy as Scripture since the second century, though Marcion's collection left it out.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a church order written as a letter of mercy
spec.body: Read straight through, 1 Timothy can seem to be a rulebook. But the letter places at its head Paul's confession that he was "the first" of sinners and was shown mercy as "a pattern" (1:15-16), and it places at its center a hymn to Christ (3:16). I suggest that the writer meant the church order to be read in that light: the rules for leaders, widows and the rich describe how a community of forgiven people keeps God's household open for others, "for every person" (2:1). This is my own reading; commentators note the importance of 1:15-16, but the claim that it governs the whole letter is mine.

prompts: Timothy reading in the house church

A sketch on an old scroll, soft edges fading into parchment: a young man stands in the courtyard of a Roman house in Ephesus, reading aloud from a papyrus letter to a small gathering of men, women, older widows and slaves seated on benches and the floor, oil lamps on ledges; the style mixes ink drawing, faint cave-drawing figures and modern line art; no hard rectangle, the scene dissolves into the scroll.
The pillar and base of the truth

On a weathered scroll, a single tall column drawn in brown ink holds up a lintel on which faint Greek letters spell 'truth'; around its base, small figures of a household (parents, children, a widow, a slave) stand together; in the far background, the vast colonnade of the temple of Artemis is sketched in pale lines; hand-drawn, soft edges, mixed ancient and modern style.

A runner and a wrestler drawn like figures on a Greek vase, in red-brown ink on parchment, with a laurel wreath above them; a faint outline of a young man holding a scroll stands beside them; the edges of the drawing fade into the scroll; no frame.
